learn: Scientists are curious. They ask questions about the world, like "Why is the sky blue?" or "Where do worms go when it rains?"
A good question is something we can try to find out by looking or testing.
Anyone can be a scientist. You just need to wonder and look closely.
check: Anyone who wonders and looks closely
Where do worms go when it rains?
lessons.try: Look out of a window and think of one question about what you see.

learn: We learn about the world with our five senses.
We see with our eyes, hear with our ears, smell with our nose, taste with our tongue and touch with our skin.
Scientists use their senses to observe. To observe means to look very carefully and notice details.
check: How many senses do we have?
lessons.try: Hold a leaf. Say what you see, feel and smell.

learn: Scientists stay safe. We only taste things a grown-up says are safe to eat.
We wash our hands after touching soil, animals or plants.
We never put things in our ears, nose or mouth during science, and we ask a grown-up for help.
check: When can we taste something in science?
Only when a grown-up says it is safe
What should we do after touching soil?
Who should we ask for help?
lessons.try: Tell a grown-up two safety rules for science time.

learn: Scientists are people who wonder about the world and try to find answers.
They ask: Why is the sky blue? Where do worms go when it rains?
Anyone who wonders and looks closely can be a scientist, even you.
check: Can a child be a scientist?
Where do worms go when it rains?
lessons.try: Tell a grown-up one thing you wonder about.

learn: Scientists look very closely. They notice small details.
A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger.
With it, you can see tiny hairs on a leaf or lines on your finger.
check: A magnifying glass makes things look...
What could you see on your fingertip?
lessons.try: Look at your fingertip with a magnifying glass, or very close. Draw what you see.

learn: Our ears tell us about the world too.
Close your eyes and listen. You may hear birds, cars, wind or people talking.
Sounds can be loud or soft, high or low.
lessons.try: Sit outside with your eyes closed for one minute. Count the different sounds.

learn: Our skin tells us if things are rough or smooth, hot or cold, hard or soft.
Sandpaper is rough. Glass is smooth. A pillow is soft.
Never touch things that could hurt you, like a hot stove.
check: Should you touch a hot stove?
lessons.try: Make a feely box. Put in three things and describe each by touch.

learn: Our nose smells and our tongue tastes.
Foods can taste sweet, salty, sour or bitter.
Scientists never taste or smell unknown things. Only taste food a grown-up gives you.
lessons.try: With a grown-up, taste a lemon, a cracker and an apple. Which is sour?

learn: Scientists use describing words: big, small, red, round, heavy, light, bumpy.
The more words you use, the better others understand.
A rock might be gray, bumpy, heavy and cold.
lessons.try: Pick an object. Use five describing words for it.

learn: Comparing means finding how things are alike and different.
An apple and a ball are both round. But the apple is food and the ball is a toy.
Scientists compare to learn more.
check: An apple and a ball are both...
lessons.try: Compare a leaf and a feather. Tell one way alike and one way different.

learn: Before testing, scientists make a guess about what will happen.
Will a rock sink or float? Most people guess sink.
A guess is okay to be wrong. Testing tells us the answer.
check: Is it okay for a guess to be wrong?
lessons.try: Guess if a spoon, a cork and a leaf will sink or float. Then test them.

learn: A test is when we try something to see what happens.
Drop a ball and a feather. Which lands first?
We watch carefully and try more than once.
check: Try something to see what happens
lessons.try: Drop two things from the same height three times. Which lands first each time?

learn: Scientists write down or draw what they see. This is called recording.
A science notebook keeps our drawings and notes.
Recording helps us remember and share.
check: Writing or drawing what we see is called...
lessons.try: Start a science notebook. Draw today's sky.

learn: Scientists use tools: magnifying glasses, rulers, scales and thermometers.
A ruler measures length. A scale measures weight. A thermometer measures temperature.
Goggles protect our eyes.
lessons.try: Find a ruler at home and measure a spoon.

learn: Scientists wonder, observe with their senses, guess, test and record.
They use tools and stay safe.
You are a scientist when you do these things!
check: A guess before a test is okay to be...
lessons.try: Do a mini test: does ice melt faster in the sun or in the shade? Record it.

learn: A push moves something away from you. A pull moves something toward you.
Pushes and pulls are called forces.
Opening a door can be a push or a pull. Kicking a ball is a push. Pulling a wagon is a pull.
lessons.try: Find three things at home you push and three things you pull.

learn: A force can make something start moving. A push starts a toy car rolling.
A force can make something stop. Your hand stops a rolling ball.
A force can change direction. A kick can send a ball a new way.
check: What can make a toy car start moving?
What happens when your hand catches a rolling ball?
A force can change a ball's...
lessons.try: Roll a ball, stop it with your hand, then push it a new way.

learn: A bigger push makes something move faster or farther.
A small push makes it move only a little.
When two things bump, they push on each other and can change how they move.
check: A big push makes a ball go...
A small push makes something move...
lessons.try: Push a ball gently, then harder. Which went farther?

learn: A push moves something away from you.
You push a door open, push a swing, push a shopping cart.
Pushing is a force.
lessons.try: Push three things gently: a ball, a toy car and a door.

learn: A pull moves something toward you.
You pull a wagon, pull open a drawer, pull a rope.
Pulling is a force too.
check: Opening a drawer is often a...
lessons.try: Pull a drawer open and pull a toy on a string.

learn: Some actions can be a push or a pull. Doors can be pushed or pulled.
Kicking is a push. Tug-of-war is a pull.
Ask: Is it going away from me or toward me?
check: To decide push or pull, ask if it goes away or...
lessons.try: Sort pictures or actions into pushes and pulls.

learn: Nothing starts moving by itself. A force starts it.
A ball sits still until you kick it.
The ball stops when the ground and air slow it down.
check: Does a ball start moving by itself?
lessons.try: Set a toy car on the floor. Does it move without a push?

learn: A push or pull can change which way something moves.
In soccer, you kick the ball to change its direction.
A ball bouncing off a wall changes direction too.
check: A push can change a ball's...
When a ball hits a wall it...
In soccer we change the ball's direction by...
lessons.try: Roll a ball at a wall. Watch it change direction.

learn: A strong push makes things go far and fast.
A gentle push makes things go a short way and slowly.
Bowling with a hard push knocks pins down better.
check: A strong push makes things go...
A gentle push makes things go...
To knock down bowling pins, push the ball...
lessons.try: Roll a ball gently, then strongly. Measure how far each goes with your steps.

learn: A ramp is a slope. Things roll down ramps.
A steeper ramp makes things roll faster.
Slides at playgrounds are ramps.
check: A steeper ramp makes things roll...
lessons.try: Make a ramp with a book and a board. Roll a car down at two heights.

learn: When moving things bump into each other, they push each other.
A rolling ball can knock down a block tower.
Bigger, faster things push harder in a crash.
check: A rolling ball can knock down a...
lessons.try: Roll a ball at a block tower. Then roll faster. What changes?

learn: A magnet can pull some metal things without touching them.
Paper clips and iron nails stick to magnets. Wood and plastic do not.
Magnets can also push other magnets away.
check: Does a magnet pick up paper?
lessons.try: Test which things a magnet picks up: a paper clip, a crayon, a spoon, a coin.

learn: Games use forces: throwing a ball is a push, pulling a sled is a pull.
Swinging needs pushes at the right time.
Every sport uses forces.
lessons.try: Name the push or pull in three games you play.

learn: Problem: a ball must go into a box. How hard should we push?
Try a gentle push. Too short? Try a bit harder.
Engineers test and change until it works.
check: If the ball stops too short, push...
To aim a ball, we change its...
lessons.try: Set a box on its side. Roll a ball in. Change your push until it works.

learn: Pushes and pulls are forces.
Forces start, stop, speed up, slow down and turn things.
Strong forces make bigger changes.
check: A strong push makes a ball go...
lessons.try: Show a push and a pull with a toy, and explain each.

learn: Living things grow and change. They need food or energy, water and air.
Living things can make more of their own kind. Cats have kittens. Plants make seeds.
People, animals and plants are all living things.
lessons.try: Name three living things you can see right now.

learn: Nonliving things do not eat, drink, breathe or grow by themselves.
Rocks, toys, chairs and water are nonliving.
A toy robot may move, but it does not eat or grow, so it is not alive.
check: Is a rock living or nonliving?
A toy robot moves. Is it alive?
No, it does not eat or grow
lessons.try: Sort pictures into living and nonliving.

learn: Some things were once alive. A dry leaf was part of a living tree.
Wood came from a tree. A shell was once the home of a living animal.
Scientists look closely to decide if something is living, nonliving or was once alive.
check: The home of a living animal
lessons.try: Find something that was once alive, like a leaf or a stick.

learn: Living things grow and change. A puppy grows into a dog.
A seed grows into a plant. A baby grows into a grown-up.
Rocks do not grow. They are nonliving.
lessons.try: Look at a baby picture of yourself. How have you grown?

lessons.t: Living Things Need Food and Water
learn: All living things need food and water.
Animals eat food. Plants make their own food from sunlight.
Without water, living things die.
lessons.try: Name the food and water you had today.

learn: Living things take in air. People and animals breathe with lungs. Fish use gills.
Plants take in air through tiny holes in their leaves.
A toy car does not breathe.
check: Plants take in air through their...
lessons.try: Put your hand on your chest and feel yourself breathe.

lessons.t: Living Things Make More of Themselves
learn: Living things have babies or make seeds.
Cats have kittens. Birds lay eggs. Trees make seeds.
That is how there are always more living things.
lessons.try: Match animal parents to their babies: cow-calf, dog-puppy, cat-kitten.

learn: Nonliving things do not grow, eat, breathe or have babies.
Rocks, water, chairs and toys are nonliving.
Some nonliving things move, like cars and wind, but they are still not alive.
check: A car moves. Is it alive?
lessons.try: Find five nonliving things in your room.

learn: Sort pictures: bird, rock, flower, shoe, fish, cup.
Living: bird, flower, fish. Nonliving: rock, shoe, cup.
Ask: Does it grow? Does it eat? Does it breathe?
lessons.try: Cut pictures from a magazine and sort them into living and nonliving.

learn: Plants are alive even though they cannot walk.
They grow, need water and air, and make seeds.
Plants turn toward the light to grow.
lessons.try: Put a plant by a window. After a few days, see which way it leans.

learn: Animals are alive. They move, eat, breathe, grow and have babies.
Animals can be big like elephants or tiny like ants.
People are animals too!
lessons.try: Watch an ant or a bird for two minutes. What does it do?

learn: Living things go through a life cycle: born, grow, have young, and die.
A frog starts as an egg, becomes a tadpole, then a frog.
A butterfly starts as an egg, then a caterpillar, a chrysalis, then a butterfly.
lessons.try: Draw the life cycle of a butterfly in four boxes.

learn: A habitat is the home where a plant or animal lives.
Fish live in water. Camels live in the desert. Monkeys live in rain forests.
Each habitat gives food, water and shelter.
check: A habitat is a living thing's...
lessons.try: Draw an animal in its habitat.

learn: Living things need care. We water plants and feed pets.
We are gentle with insects and leave birds' nests alone.
Caring for living things keeps them healthy.
check: How do we care for plants?
Caring for living things keeps them...
lessons.try: Water a plant or feed a pet with a grown-up.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Living Things
learn: Living things grow, need food and water, breathe and have young.
Nonliving things do not.
Living things go through life cycles and live in habitats.
lessons.try: Go outside. List three living and three nonliving things you see.

learn: Plants are living things. They need sunlight, water and air to grow.
Many plants also grow in soil, which holds them up and gives them water.
A plant with no water wilts and droops. Water helps it stand tall again.
check: What happens to a plant with no water?
What does soil do for many plants?
Holds them up and gives water
lessons.try: Water a plant and watch how it looks over a few days.

learn: Plants make their own food. They use sunlight to do it.
That is why plants grow toward the light. A plant on a windowsill bends to the window.
Animals cannot make their own food this way. They need to eat.
check: What do plants use to make food?
A plant on a windowsill bends toward...
Can animals make food from sunlight like plants?
lessons.try: Put a plant by a window. Turn it after a week and watch it bend back.

learn: Roots take in water from the soil and hold the plant in place.
The stem holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves.
Leaves catch the sunlight to make food.
check: Which part takes in water from the soil?
Holds the plant up and carries water
lessons.try: Draw a plant and label the roots, stem and leaves.

learn: Most plants start as seeds.
Seeds come in many sizes: tiny poppy seeds, big avocado seeds, and coconuts.
A seed has a baby plant and food inside.
check: Inside a seed is a baby plant and...
Which is a very big seed?
lessons.try: Look at seeds from an apple, a bean and a sunflower. Compare them.

learn: To plant a seed, put it in soil, cover it lightly and water it.
Keep the soil damp but not flooded.
In a few days, a sprout pokes out.
check: To plant a seed, put it in...
The first green part to poke out is a...
lessons.try: Plant a bean seed in a cup with soil. Water it and watch.

learn: Plants need light to make food and grow.
A plant in a dark closet turns yellow and weak.
Window sills are good spots for plants.
check: A plant kept in the dark turns...
A good place for a plant is a...
lessons.try: Put one plant in the light and one in a dark box for a week. Compare.

learn: Plants drink water through their roots.
Too little water makes them droop. Too much can rot the roots.
Check the soil with your finger before watering.
check: Before watering, check the soil with your...
lessons.try: Feel the soil of a plant. Is it dry or damp?

learn: Plants need air, just like animals.
They also need space so their roots and leaves can spread.
Plants that are too crowded grow small.
lessons.try: Plant three seeds close together and three far apart. Compare later.

learn: Roots grow under the ground.
They hold the plant in place and soak up water.
Carrots and radishes are roots we eat.
check: Which is a root we eat?
lessons.try: Gently pull a weed and look at its roots.

learn: The stem holds the plant up.
Water travels up the stem like a straw.
A tree trunk is a big, woody stem.
check: Water travels up the stem like a...
lessons.try: Put celery in colored water. After a day, look at the leaves.

learn: Leaves catch sunlight to make food for the plant.
Leaves come in many shapes: round, pointed, long and thin.
Lettuce and spinach are leaves we eat.
check: Which is a leaf we eat?
lessons.try: Collect three different leaves. Trace their shapes.

learn: Flowers make seeds. Bees help by carrying pollen from flower to flower.
After a flower, a fruit may grow. The fruit holds the seeds.
Apples, tomatoes and peppers are fruits with seeds inside.
lessons.try: Cut open an apple with a grown-up. Count the seeds.

learn: Plants grow from seed to sprout to young plant to grown plant.
Grown plants make flowers and seeds, and the cycle starts again.
We can measure how tall a plant grows.
check: We can track plant growth by...
lessons.try: Measure your bean plant every few days with a ruler or paper strip.

learn: We eat many parts of plants: roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.
Broccoli is a flower. Peas are seeds. Celery is a stem.
Eating plants keeps us healthy.
lessons.try: Look at your dinner. Which plant parts are on your plate?

learn: Plants need light, water, air and space.
Plants have roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits.
Plants grow from seeds and make new seeds.
check: Which part holds the plant up?
What do plants need to make food?
lessons.try: Draw a plant and label its roots, stem, leaves and flower.

learn: Animals need food, water, air and a safe place to live called a shelter.
A bird builds a nest. A rabbit digs a burrow. A bear rests in a den.
Animals cannot make their own food, so they must find it.
check: Where does a bird often live?
Can animals make their own food?
lessons.try: Name an animal and its shelter.

learn: Some animals eat plants, like cows, rabbits and deer.
Some animals eat other animals, like lions and owls.
Some eat both plants and animals, like bears and people.
lessons.try: Sort animals into plant eaters, meat eaters and both.

learn: Pets are animals that live with people. They need care every day.
A pet needs fresh water, the right food, a clean home and gentle love.
Some animals are wild. We watch wild animals from a distance and do not touch them.
check: What does a pet need every day?
Fresh water and the right food
What should we do with wild animals?
lessons.try: Make a list of what a dog or cat needs each day.

learn: Animals need food for energy to move and grow.
Cows eat grass. Cats eat meat. Bears eat both plants and meat.
Animals find their food in their habitat.
lessons.try: Name the food your favorite animal eats.

learn: Animals drink water from rivers, ponds, puddles and bowls.
Some desert animals get water from the food they eat.
Animals cannot live long without water.
check: Some desert animals get water from their...
Can animals live long without water?
lessons.try: Put a shallow dish of water outside. Watch who visits.

learn: Animals breathe air to live.
Land animals use lungs. Fish use gills to get air from water.
Whales live in water but come up to breathe air.
lessons.try: Watch a fish in a tank. Look at its gills open and close.

learn: Shelter keeps animals safe from weather and danger.
Birds build nests. Rabbits dig burrows. Bees live in hives.
People live in houses, which are shelters too.
lessons.try: Find a shelter an animal made near your home, like a nest or a web.

learn: Animals that eat only plants are called herbivores.
Deer, rabbits, cows and elephants are plant eaters.
They have flat teeth for chewing plants.
check: Animals that eat only plants are...
Plant eaters have teeth that are...
lessons.try: Look at a picture of a cow's teeth. Are they flat or pointy?

learn: Animals that eat other animals are called carnivores.
Lions, wolves, sharks and owls are meat eaters.
They often have sharp teeth or claws.
lessons.try: Look at a picture of a lion's teeth. What shape are they?

learn: Some animals eat both plants and meat. They are called omnivores.
Bears, raccoons, chickens and people are omnivores.
They have different kinds of teeth.
check: Animals that eat both plants and meat are...
lessons.try: List what you ate yesterday. Were you an omnivore?

learn: Animals move to find food, water and shelter.
Fish swim. Birds fly. Snakes slither. Kangaroos hop.
Their bodies are made for the way they move.
lessons.try: Move like three animals: hop like a frog, slither like a snake, fly like a bird.

learn: Animals have coverings that protect them.
Birds have feathers. Fish have scales. Bears have fur. Turtles have shells.
Coverings keep animals warm, dry or safe.
lessons.try: Touch a feather and fur (or pictures). Describe how each feels.

learn: Many animals care for their young.
A mother bird feeds her chicks. A kangaroo carries her joey in her pouch.
Some baby animals, like turtles, take care of themselves from the start.
check: Do some babies care for themselves from the start?
lessons.try: Find out what a baby kangaroo, owl and whale are called.

learn: Some animals sleep through winter. This is called hibernation. Bears and some frogs hibernate.
Some animals fly to warm places. This is called migration. Many birds migrate.
Some animals grow thick fur and stay.
check: Birds flying to warm places is...
lessons.try: Draw one animal that hibernates and one that migrates.

learn: Animals need food, water, air and shelter.
They can be plant eaters, meat eaters or both.
Animals move, have coverings and care for their young in many ways.
lessons.try: Choose an animal and tell what it eats, where it lives and how it moves.

units.t: Plants and Animals Change Their World

learn: Living things change the places they live.
A squirrel digs holes to hide nuts. Some nuts it forgets grow into new trees.
Beavers cut trees with their teeth and build dams across streams. The dam makes a pond.
check: What can a forgotten nut become?
lessons.try: Look outside for signs that an animal changed something: holes, nests or tracks.

learn: Plant roots can grow into cracks and break rocks or sidewalks.
Trees give shade and homes to birds and insects.
Fallen leaves rot and make the soil rich for new plants.
check: What can roots do to a sidewalk?
Fallen leaves help make the soil...
lessons.try: Find a crack in a sidewalk with a plant growing in it.

learn: People change the land too. We build roads, houses and farms.
Some changes can hurt plants and animals, like litter and dirty water.
People can also help: plant trees, pick up trash and make parks.
check: How can people help the land?
Plant trees and pick up trash
lessons.try: Think of one way you can help the land near your home.

learn: Beavers cut down small trees with their teeth.
They pile sticks and mud across a stream to make a dam.
The dam makes a pond where the beaver builds its lodge.
lessons.try: Build a small dam with sticks and clay in a tray of water.

learn: Squirrels bury nuts to eat later.
They forget some, and those nuts grow into new trees.
So squirrels help forests grow.
lessons.try: Bury a seed in a pot like a squirrel. Water it and wait.

learn: Earthworms dig tunnels in the soil.
Tunnels let air and water reach plant roots.
Worms also eat dead leaves and make the soil rich.
lessons.try: Gently dig in a garden and look for worms. Put them back.

learn: Birds gather twigs, grass, mud and feathers to build nests.
Each kind of bird builds its own kind of nest.
Some birds even use string or bits of paper.
check: Do all birds build the same nest?
lessons.try: Leave short pieces of yarn outside in spring. Watch if birds take them.

learn: Ants dig rooms and tunnels underground.
They carry dirt up and pile it into an anthill.
Thousands of ants work together.
lessons.try: Watch an anthill from a safe distance. Do not touch it.

learn: Plant roots can grow into cracks in rocks and sidewalks.
As roots grow, they push and can split the rock or lift the sidewalk.
Plants are stronger than they look!
lessons.try: Look for a sidewalk crack with a plant growing in it.

learn: Plant roots hold soil in place.
Without plants, rain can wash soil away.
People plant grass on hills to stop soil from sliding.
check: Without plants, rain can wash soil...
People plant grass on hills to stop...
lessons.try: Pour water on a tray of bare soil and a tray of grass. Which loses more soil?

learn: People change land to build houses, roads and schools.
They cut trees, flatten hills and dig foundations.
People need homes, but we should leave room for plants and animals.
check: Should we leave room for plants and animals?
lessons.try: Draw your street. What did people build there?

learn: Farmers plow fields and plant crops like corn, wheat and vegetables.
Farms change land from forests or grass into fields.
Farms feed many people.
lessons.try: Find out where one food in your kitchen was grown.

learn: Elephants knock down trees and make paths.
Their paths help other animals move through the forest.
Elephants also spread seeds in their dung.
lessons.try: Draw an elephant making a path through trees.

learn: People can change land in good ways too.
We can plant trees, make gardens and clean up parks.
Gardens give food to people, bees and butterflies.
check: A good way to change land is to...
lessons.try: Plant a flower for bees in a pot or garden.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Changing the World
learn: Animals change their world: beavers build dams, worms dig, birds build nests.
Plants change their world: roots break rocks and hold soil.
People change the world, and we can help it too.
check: A way people help land is to...
lessons.try: Tell one way an animal, a plant and a person changes the land.

learn: The sun is a star. It is very far away and very big.
The sun gives us light and heat.
Never look straight at the sun. It can hurt your eyes.
check: What does the sun give us?
Is it safe to look straight at the sun?
lessons.try: Feel a window on a sunny day. Is it warm?

learn: Sunlight warms the land, water and air.
A sidewalk in the sun feels hotter than one in the shade.
Shade is a place where something blocks the sunlight, like a tree or an umbrella.
check: Which feels hotter on a sunny day?
lessons.try: Touch a sunny spot and a shady spot outside. Which is warmer?

learn: We can stay cool in the shade on a hot day.
Hats, sunglasses and sunscreen protect us from too much sun.
People build roofs and plant trees to make shade.
check: What protects your skin from the sun?
Where can we stay cool on a hot day?
Why do people plant trees near houses?
lessons.try: Design a shade for a toy using paper and sticks.

learn: The sun lights up our day.
When our side of Earth faces the sun, it is day. When it faces away, it is night.
Never look straight at the sun. It can hurt your eyes.
check: Should we look straight at the sun?
When our side faces away from the sun, it is...
lessons.try: Draw daytime and nighttime. What is in the sky in each?

learn: Sunlight warms the land, water, air and us.
Sand at the beach gets hot in the sun.
Places with lots of sun are often warm.
check: A rock in the sun is ___ than one in the shade.
lessons.try: Feel a rock in the sun and a rock in the shade. Which is warmer?

learn: A shadow forms when something blocks the light.
Your shadow is dark and shaped like you.
Shadows are long in the morning and evening, and short at noon.
check: A shadow forms when something blocks...
lessons.try: Go outside in the morning and at noon. Compare your shadow.

learn: Shade is a place where sunlight is blocked.
Trees, umbrellas and roofs make shade.
Standing in the shade on a hot day keeps you cooler.
check: On a hot day, shade keeps you...
lessons.try: Find three places that make shade at the park or school.

learn: Sun can melt ice, chocolate and crayons.
Melting is when something solid turns soft or liquid from heat.
Ice melts into water.
lessons.try: Put an ice cube in the sun and one in the shade. Which melts first?

learn: Dark colors soak up more sunlight and get warmer.
Light colors bounce sunlight away and stay cooler.
That is why people wear light clothes in summer.
check: Which gets warmer in the sun?
lessons.try: Put a black paper and a white paper in the sun. Feel them after 10 minutes.

learn: The sun warms water in puddles, lakes and oceans.
When water warms, some of it rises into the air. Puddles dry up.
That water later falls as rain.
check: When the sun warms a puddle, it...
Water that rises into the air later falls as...
lessons.try: Draw a chalk line around a puddle. Check it later. What happened?

learn: Plants use sunlight to make food.
Plants grow toward the sun.
Sunflowers turn their heads to follow the sun when young.
lessons.try: Put a plant near a window for a week. Which way does it lean?

learn: Too much sun can burn our skin.
Wear a hat, sunscreen and sunglasses.
Drink water and rest in the shade on hot days.
lessons.try: Pack a sun safety bag: hat, sunscreen, water bottle, sunglasses.

learn: Engineers can design shade structures to keep things cool.
A shade needs a top that blocks light and legs to hold it up.
Test it: is the ground under it cooler?
check: A shade needs a top that blocks...
To test a shade, check if under it is...
lessons.try: Build a small shade for a toy with paper and sticks. Test it with an ice cube.

learn: The sun is very, very far from Earth.
It is a huge star, much bigger than Earth.
It looks small because it is so far away.
check: The sun looks small because it is...
Compared to Earth, the sun is...
lessons.try: Look at a ball close up, then far away. Does it look smaller far away?

lessons.t: Show What You Know: The Sun
learn: The sun gives light and heat.
Sunlight makes shadows, melts ice and helps plants grow.
Shade keeps things cool, and we stay safe in the sun.
lessons.try: Explain to a grown-up why ice melts faster in the sun.

learn: Weather is what the air outside is like right now.
It can be sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy or snowy.
We look out of the window and feel the air to tell the weather.
check: What the air outside is like right now
Which is a kind of weather?
How can we tell the weather?
Look outside and feel the air
lessons.try: Look outside and say today's weather.

learn: A thermometer tells how hot or cold it is.
A rain gauge catches rain to show how much fell.
Scientists who study weather are called meteorologists.
check: What tells how hot or cold it is?
What catches rain to measure it?
lessons.try: Put a cup outside on a rainy day. How much rain did it catch?

learn: Weather changes from day to day.
We can keep a weather chart and look for patterns, like more rainy days in spring.
Weather helps us choose what to wear: a coat for cold, a hat for sun, boots for rain.
check: Does weather change from day to day?
What should you wear on a rainy day?
What can a weather chart show?
lessons.try: Keep a weather chart for one week.

learn: On a sunny day, the sky is clear and the sun shines.
Sunny days can be warm or even cold in winter.
Sunny weather is good for playing outside.
check: On a sunny day the sky is...
A sunny day is good for...
lessons.try: Draw a sunny day and what you would do.

learn: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water.
Some clouds are white and puffy. Dark gray clouds may bring rain.
A cloudy sky can hide the sun.
lessons.try: Look at the clouds today. What shapes do you see?

learn: Rain falls from clouds when the water drops get heavy.
Rain fills rivers and helps plants grow.
We wear raincoats and boots in the rain.
lessons.try: Put a cup outside on a rainy day. How much rain does it catch?

learn: When it is very cold, water in clouds freezes into snowflakes.
Every snowflake has six sides.
We wear coats, hats and mittens in the snow.
lessons.try: Make a paper snowflake by folding and cutting paper.

learn: Wind is moving air. We cannot see it, but we see what it moves.
Wind moves leaves, kites and flags.
Strong wind can knock things over.
check: No, but we see what it moves
lessons.try: Make a pinwheel or fly a kite on a windy day.

learn: Temperature tells how hot or cold the air is.
A thermometer measures temperature. The red line goes up when it is hot.
We dress for the temperature.
check: A thermometer's line goes ___ when it is hot.
Temperature tells how ___ the air is.
lessons.try: Read a thermometer outside in the morning and afternoon.

learn: A thermometer measures temperature. A rain gauge measures rain. A wind sock shows wind direction.
Weather scientists are called meteorologists.
They use tools to tell us the weather.
lessons.try: Make a rain gauge from a clear cup and a ruler.

learn: We can record the weather each day on a chart.
Use pictures: a sun, a cloud, rain drops, a snowflake.
At the end of the month, count which weather happened most.
check: A weather chart records the weather each...
At the end of the month we can count which weather happened...
lessons.try: Make a weather chart and fill it in every day for a week.

learn: A weather report tells us what the weather will be.
It is on TV, radio and apps.
It helps us plan: bring an umbrella or wear sunscreen.
check: A weather report tells what the weather...
If rain is coming, bring an...
lessons.try: Watch or listen to a weather report with a grown-up.

learn: We choose clothes for the weather.
Rain: raincoat and boots. Snow: coat, hat, mittens. Sun: hat and sunscreen.
Dressing right keeps us healthy.
lessons.try: Dress a paper doll for a snowy day and a sunny day.

learn: Animals act differently in different weather.
Birds fluff their feathers in cold. Dogs pant when hot.
Some animals hide before storms.
check: Birds fluff feathers when it is...
lessons.try: Watch a pet or bird in hot and cold weather. What do they do?

learn: Weather can be sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy or windy.
We measure weather with tools and record it on charts.
We dress and plan for the weather.
lessons.try: Be a weather reporter. Tell your family today's weather.

learn: There are four seasons: spring, summer, fall and winter.
They come in the same order every year.
In many places summer is warm, winter is cold, and spring and fall are in between.
lessons.try: Draw a tree in each of the four seasons.

learn: In spring, many plants grow new leaves and flowers.
In fall, leaves change colour and drop in many places.
Some animals sleep through winter, and some birds fly to warmer places.
check: When do many plants grow new flowers?
When do leaves change colour and drop?
What do some birds do in winter?
lessons.try: Name one thing that happens in fall.

learn: Some weather is dangerous: thunderstorms, tornadoes, hurricanes and blizzards.
Weather forecasters warn people so they can get ready.
In a storm, stay inside with a grown-up, away from windows. When thunder roars, go indoors.
lessons.try: Make a storm safety plan with a grown-up.

learn: In spring, the weather gets warmer.
Plants sprout, flowers bloom and baby animals are born.
Spring has rain showers.
check: Many baby animals are born in...
lessons.try: Find signs of spring: buds, flowers, birds.

learn: Summer is the hottest season.
Days are long and nights are short.
People swim, play outside and eat cold treats.
lessons.try: List three things you like to do in summer.

learn: In fall, the weather gets cooler.
Many leaves change color and fall from trees.
Farmers harvest crops like pumpkins and apples.
lessons.try: Collect fall leaves of different colors.

learn: Winter is the coldest season.
In many places it snows. Days are short and nights are long.
Some animals hibernate.
lessons.try: Draw what you wear in winter.

learn: The seasons go in a circle: spring, summer, fall, winter, then spring again.
This circle repeats every year.
Each season lasts about three months.
lessons.try: Draw the four seasons in a circle.

learn: Many trees change with the seasons.
Spring: buds. Summer: green leaves. Fall: colorful leaves. Winter: bare branches.
Evergreen trees stay green all year.
lessons.try: Pick a tree near you. Draw it in each season.

learn: Thunderstorms bring rain, lightning and thunder.
Lightning is a giant spark. Thunder is the sound it makes.
When thunder roars, go indoors.
lessons.try: Practice: say When thunder roars, go indoors!

learn: A snowstorm, or blizzard, has heavy snow and strong wind.
It can be hard to see, and roads get slippery.
Stay inside and keep warm.
check: A blizzard has heavy snow and strong...
In a snowstorm, it is best to...
lessons.try: Make a list of things to have at home for a snowstorm.

learn: Hurricanes are huge storms that form over warm oceans.
Tornadoes are spinning winds that touch the ground.
Weather scientists warn people so they can stay safe.
lessons.try: Spin water in a jar to see a tornado shape (with a grown-up).

learn: Families make a plan for storms.
Know the safe room, keep a flashlight, water and snacks.
Listen to grown-ups and weather warnings.
check: A storm kit should have a...
A safe room is where you go during a...
lessons.try: Make a storm kit list with your family.

learn: Not every place has four seasons the same way.
Near the equator, it is warm all year. Some places have a rainy season and a dry season.
In the far north, winters are very long.
check: Some places have a rainy and a ___ season.
In the far north, winters are...
lessons.try: Find a warm country and a cold country on a globe.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Seasons and Storms
learn: The four seasons are spring, summer, fall and winter.
Storms include thunderstorms, snowstorms, hurricanes and tornadoes.
We stay safe by planning and listening to warnings.
lessons.try: Tell a grown-up your favorite season and how to stay safe in a storm.

learn: Living things need clean air, clean water and land.
Reduce means using less. Turn off the water while you brush your teeth.
Turn off lights when you leave a room to save energy.
check: Turn it off while brushing teeth
What should you do when leaving a room?
lessons.try: Find two ways your family can use less water or electricity.

learn: Reuse means using something again.
A jar can hold crayons. A box can become a toy house.
Fixing a toy instead of throwing it away is reusing too.
check: How can a jar be reused?
lessons.try: Make something new from an old box or jar.

learn: Recycle means making old things into new things.
Paper, cans and some plastic can be recycled.
We put them in the recycling bin so a factory can make them into new things.
check: Making old things into new things
lessons.try: Sort clean trash into recycling and not recycling.

learn: Earth is the planet where we live with plants and animals.
It gives us air, water, food and land.
We must take care of it.
lessons.try: Draw Earth and the things it gives us.

learn: Natural resources are things from nature that we use.
Water, trees, soil, rocks and air are natural resources.
We make paper from trees and bricks from clay.
lessons.try: Find three things at home made from natural resources.

learn: Clean water is precious.
Turn off the tap while brushing teeth. Take short showers.
Fix drips and use only what you need.
lessons.try: Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth for one week.

learn: Energy powers lights, TVs and cars.
Turn off lights when you leave a room.
Walking or biking saves energy too.
check: When you leave a room, turn off the...
lessons.try: Be the light monitor at home: turn off lights in empty rooms.

learn: Litter is trash left on the ground.
Animals can get stuck in plastic or eat trash and get sick.
Always put trash in a trash can.
check: Litter is trash left on the...
lessons.try: With gloves and a grown-up, pick up litter at a park.

learn: Composting turns food scraps and leaves into rich soil.
Worms and tiny living things break the scraps down.
Compost helps gardens grow.
lessons.try: Start a small compost jar with leaves and fruit peels.

learn: Trees give us shade, clean air and homes for animals.
Planting a tree helps Earth for many years.
Arbor Day is a day for planting trees.
lessons.try: Plant a seed or small tree with your family or class.

learn: Some animals are in danger because their homes are disappearing.
People protect animals by saving forests, oceans and wetlands.
Zoos and parks help some animals too.
check: Some animals are in danger because their ___ are disappearing.
People can protect animals by saving...
lessons.try: Learn about one animal that needs our help.

learn: Smoke from cars and factories can make air dirty.
Plants help clean the air.
Walking, biking and planting trees help keep air clean.
check: Biking instead of driving keeps air...
lessons.try: Count how many trips your family could walk or bike this week.

learn: Using less means only taking what we need.
Use both sides of paper. Take only the food you will eat.
Using less makes less trash.
check: Using less means taking only what we...
lessons.try: Use both sides of your paper for a whole day.

learn: Earth Day is on April 22.
On Earth Day, people clean up, plant trees and learn about nature.
Every day can be Earth Day when we care.
lessons.try: Make an Earth Day poster that tells one way to help.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Caring for Earth
learn: We reduce, reuse and recycle.
We save water and energy and keep litter off the ground.
Small actions every day help our whole planet.
lessons.try: Make a promise card: three things you will do to help Earth.
